tldr: In humanoid motion tracking, introducing a physics-informed world model—where a neural network predicts contact wrenches (contact forces and moments) and the next state is computed in closed form using known rigid-body dynamics equations—substantially improves tracking performance for complex motions involving contact changes.
hero_caption: Overview of the DynaMimic framework. (a) Given the current state and action, the model predicts contact wrenches for each candidate support link and residual forces, then analytically computes the next state via known forward dynamics. (b) The world model is trained on trajectories and link wrenches collected from a simulator. (c) Policy gradients are backpropagated through imagined rollouts in the frozen world model to optimize a highly accurate tracking policy.
overview:
Enabling humanoid robots to reproduce diverse skills from human demonstrations through "whole-body motion tracking" is an essential capability for creating general-purpose robots that can walk, recover from the floor, and perform parkour. However, training policies on large-scale motion libraries with model-free reinforcement learning either requires massive computing clusters or causes performance degradation when distilling motion specialists into a single generalist model. Prior work, SuperMimic, drastically reduced this computational cost by learning a differentiable neural network world model (an environment transition model) and running short imagined rollouts inside it. Yet, because it forced the network to memorize all physical behaviors—including contact—as a black box, prediction errors spiked during changes of support (such as touching hands to or lifting them from the floor), leading to unstable policy optimization.

To tackle this, the authors adopted a simple insight: since the robot's equations of motion and rigid-body parameters like link inertia are already known, the network only needs to predict the unknown contact forces. This led to their proposed method, "DynaMimic." The neural network outputs only the contact wrench (forces and moments) at each candidate support link alongside a residual generalized force to capture unmodeled dynamics, while the next state is integrated in closed form (analytically) using Lagrangian forward dynamics equations. Furthermore, by conditioning on local terrain height maps, it handles physical interactions with uneven terrain and obstacles.

Evaluations across 60 full LAFAN1 motions show that DynaMimic reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 18.6% relative to SuperMimic. It achieves especially notable improvements on dynamic motions involving non-foot contacts, such as recovering from the floor. Deployed on a physical A3 humanoid, the learned policy successfully executes diverse skills including floor recovery, cartwheels, and box vaults.
contributions: Proposed a physics-informed differentiable world model that uses a network to predict only contact wrenches and residual forces, while computing the next state analytically through known forward dynamics equations.
Leveraged contact wrenches computed internally by the simulator directly as supervision signals, enabling accurate learning of link-level load distribution without manual annotation.
Incorporated local height maps into both the policy and the world model to handle physical contact interactions with geometric obstacles such as steps and vaults.
Directly deployed the learned policies onto a real A3 humanoid, demonstrating agile, complex whole-body contact motions such as floor recovery, cartwheels, and box vaults.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need to Reintroduce Physics into the World Model?
sections.summary: In humanoid motion tracking for learning diverse skills from human demonstrations, heavy computational cost has been the primary bottleneck. While prior differentiable world models cut computational demands, treating contact physics as a black box led to accumulating errors during changes of support. To solve this, DynaMimic explicitly embeds known dynamics equations.
sections.details:
Having a single policy enable a humanoid robot to walk like a human, get back up after falling, and jump over obstacles has long been a dream in robotics. However, achieving this through model-free reinforcement learning (RL) required either training specialist policies for individual motions and distilling them, or running massive compute clusters for days.

A method called SuperMimic drastically lowered this computational cost. By training a "differentiable world model" that mimics simulator transitions and rolling it forward in time to backpropagate gradients, it optimized policies efficiently. However, there was a major pitfall. Traditional world models used an end-to-end structure that directly predicted the "next state" from the current state and action, failing to capture discrete contact switches.

Consider a floor recovery motion. When hands are on the floor, extending the elbows lifts the upper body. But right after the hands leave the ground, taking the exact same action simply extends the arms in mid-air. The body's physical response changes completely once the contact state flips. Implicit models miss predictions at these contact boundaries, and those errors compound across rollouts, steering policy updates in the wrong direction.

Yet, no matter how contact forces shift, the Newton-Euler equations governing the robot's body stay the same. As long as the current state, motor torques, and external forces from the ground are known, subsequent accelerations can be calculated strictly through analytical formulas. DynaMimic therefore adopts a hybrid design: let the network predict only the unknown contact forces and residual forces (such as joint friction), and update the state using analytical equations of motion. Furthermore, by using the simulator's internal contact wrenches as supervisory training targets, the model learns contact physics without requiring extra manual labels.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Motion Tracking and Physics-Informed World Models
sections.summary: Humanoid motion tracking has evolved from RL methods like PPO to off-policy replay and world models. Meanwhile, vision and graphics research has actively leveraged physics constraints for motion recovery. DynaMimic combines the strengths of both domains to learn robotic control policies.
sections.details:
The modern history of humanoid motion tracking took off with DeepMimic, which used PPO (a policy gradient method) to track reference motions. This was followed by PHC, capable of handling large-scale motion libraries; PULSE, which learned latent action spaces; and MaskedMimic, which generated motions from partial joint tracks. Real-robot deployments have also advanced, with H2O and OmniH2O achieving whole-body teleoperation, HOVER handling diverse instructions, and BeyondMimic enabling agile behaviors.

However, these methods consume massive amounts of environment interaction data. As a result, off-policy approaches utilizing replay buffers (such as FlashSAC) and model-based techniques predicting environment behavior (such as DayDreamer) gained traction. SuperMimic brought this concept to humanoid motion tracking, achieving dramatic training speedups through short imagined rollouts inside a differentiable dynamics model. Nevertheless, as noted earlier, it suffered from modeling contact physics only implicitly.

On the other hand, research on estimating and generating human motion in computer vision has actively embraced "physics-informed" ideas by explicitly embedding ground contact constraints and dynamics models. PROX and WHAM enforce foot contacts to prevent foot sliding, while works like NeuralSim propose hybrid simulators that embed learned modules into differentiable rigid-body dynamics.

DynaMimic's novelty lies in bringing this hybrid design philosophy directly into the humanoid "tracking policy training loop." Instead of merely approximating state transitions, it explicitly predicts wrenches for individual contact links and solves them with rigid-body dynamics, enabling accurate gradients to backpropagate to the policy.

sections.heading: How Are Physics Dynamics and Neural Networks Combined?
sections.summary: DynaMimic iterates through three steps: data collection in the simulator, world model training, and policy updates via imagined rollouts. The world model predicts wrenches and residual forces across 15 candidate support links, computing the next state using closed-form rigid-body dynamics equations. A constraint layer prevents non-physical forces from emerging.
sections.details:
The overall architecture alternates through data collection, model learning, and policy optimization. Here is a step-by-step look at these three core components.

### 3.1 Training Loop
Training loops through three sequential stages:
- 1. The current policy runs in the simulator, storing state trajectories, executed actions, and observed link contact wrenches into a replay buffer.
- 2. Short transition windows are sampled from the buffer, and the world model $f_\phi$ is trained on the recorded actions.
- 3. With the world model parameters $\phi$ frozen, the policy selects actions to run 32-step "imagined rollouts" inside the model, backpropagating the resulting reward gradients to update policy $\pi_\theta$.

Policy inputs consist of 10 historical proprioceptive steps (joint positions, velocities, etc.) and reference motion frames. For terrain tracking, the policy also receives a robot-centric local height map $P_t$ ($21\times 21$ grid, 0.1 m resolution).

### 3.2 Learning a Physics-Informed World Model
The world model $f_\phi$ is split into a force predictor $\mathcal{F}_\phi$ and an analytical rigid-body integrator $I_{\mathrm{phys}}$.
- **Predicting Contact Wrenches**: Across the robot's 15 candidate support links $\mathcal{C}$, the model predicts contact wrenches $W_t$ (3D forces + 3D moments) at each of 4 sub-steps (5 ms each) within a 20 ms control step. It also outputs a 35-dimensional residual generalized force $\tau_{\mathrm{res},t}$ to absorb modeling errors such as joint friction.
- **Physically Constrained Output Layer**: To prevent the network from generating arbitrary forces, its outputs are bounded mathematically. Normal force must be non-negative ($F_z \geq 0$), tangential force must stay within the friction cone ($\|F_{xy}\|_2 \leq \mu F_z$, where $\mu$ is the friction coefficient), and moments are bounded proportionally to normal force. This fundamentally eliminates non-physical artifacts like "the ground pulling on the robot."
- **State Prediction via Forward Dynamics**: The predicted contact wrenches are mapped to joint-torque space via the transposed Jacobian $J^\top$ and summed with PD control motor torques $\tau_{\mathrm{act}}$, passive damping $\tau_{\mathrm{pass}}$, and residual forces $\tau_{\mathrm{res}}$. Then, using semi-implicit Euler integration with the generalized mass matrix $M$ and Coriolis/gravity vector $h$, the next joint positions and velocities $(Q_{t+1}, \nu_{t+1})$ are computed analytically across two 10 ms integration steps.
- **Model Training Loss**: The loss combines the trajectory squared error $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{traj}}$, the wrench error against simulator measurements $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wrench}}$, and a regularization term penalizing large residual forces $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{res}}$. Directly supervising with ground-truth wrenches ensures the model accurately learns weight distribution across both feet during double-support phases.

### 3.3 Learning the Tracking Policy
To update the policy, imagined rollouts unroll 32 steps forward inside the frozen world model. The policy maximizes the total return, which combines per-step tracking rewards (pose tracking, action smoothness, joint limit avoidance) with bootstrapped values from a Critic estimating value at the rollout horizon. During backpropagation through time (BPTT), gradients cleanly flow through rigid-body dynamics and the wrench predictor directly to policy weights, enabling highly stable updates. During real-robot deployment, the world model and Critic are discarded, leaving only the lightweight policy $\pi_\theta$ to run standalone.

(a) The network $\mathcal{F}_\phi$ predicts contact wrenches $W_t$ and residual forces, passing them to the analytical rigid-body integrator $I_{\mathrm{phys}}$ to compute the next state. (b) The model is trained on trajectories and wrenches from the buffer. (c) The policy runs imagined rollouts inside the frozen model, computing policy gradients via BPTT.

sections.heading: Superior Tracking on Benchmarks and Acrobatics on the Real Humanoid
sections.summary: DynaMimic was compared against SuperMimic on LAFAN1 as well as uneven terrain and parkour datasets. DynaMimic cut tracking error (MPJPE) by 10% to over 18%, widening the gap especially on motions with abrupt contact changes. Ablations confirmed that adding forward dynamics is the most crucial component, and the real A3 humanoid successfully executed varied skills.
sections.details:
Experiments were run on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU. Primary evaluation metrics included mean per-joint position error across all joints (MPJPE, mm), pelvis-relative joint position error (Root-relative MPJPE, mm), joint velocity/acceleration errors, normalized return, and 7-step open-loop world model prediction error (WM MSE).

### 4.1 Flat-Ground Results on LAFAN1
Across 60 LAFAN1 sequences and 18 challenging segments, DynaMimic was evaluated against baseline SuperMimic. DynaMimic achieved an overall 18.6% reduction in MPJPE relative to SuperMimic. Comparing learning curves shows that DynaMimic consistently maintains lower world model prediction error (WM MSE) and higher normalized returns throughout training.

### 4.2 Breakdown by Contact Modes
Categorizing LAFAN1 motions into four quadrants based on "presence of non-foot contacts" and "low vs. high motion intensity" highlights DynaMimic's true strengths. While DynaMimic outperformed the baseline across all categories, the gap was most pronounced in the "non-foot contacts × high intensity" quadrant. SuperMimic failed mid-motion during floor recovery, terminating at 2.22 seconds, whereas DynaMimic tracked the entire 10-second sequence from rolling over, pushing up with hands, to stepping onto one knee and standing up.

### 4.3 Terrain-Conditioned Tracking (A3 Parkour & GRAIL)
Evaluations on terrain where local height maps were provided as input demonstrated similar advantages:
- **A3 Parkour (22 motions)**: Climbing and vaulting using boxes. MPJPE dropped by 14.9%, from 66.15 mm down to 56.28 mm. SuperMimic failed to follow lateral leg swings during box vaults, while DynaMimic accurately tracked hand placement and dynamic leg swings.
- **GRAIL (9,736 clips)**: Locomotion over curbs, slopes, and stairs. MPJPE decreased by 10.8%, from 141.88 mm to 126.57 mm, alongside improved task completion rates.

### 4.4 Ablation Study
Ablating individual components revealed the following insights:
- Removing contact wrench supervision degrades tracking accuracy.
- Removing relative position and velocity inputs of candidate links also harms performance.
- The largest performance drop came from "removing forward dynamics." Without it, returns plummeted and all error metrics spiked. This confirms that explicitly integrating the rigid-body physics model is the single most critical driver of performance.

### 4.5 Deployment to the Real A3 Humanoid
Learned policies were transferred sim-to-real onto the physical A3 humanoid. Operating without the world model, the single policy successfully executed challenging acrobatic skills involving multi-body contact with the ground and obstacles: floor recovery from a fallen state, cartwheels, and box vaults in the real world.

captions.F4: Tracking comparison on a LAFAN1 floor recovery motion. DynaMimic successfully tracks the full 10-second sequence—rolling to the side, pushing up off the floor with hands, kneeling on one knee, and standing up. In contrast, SuperMimic falls mid-motion, terminating its rollout at 2.22 seconds.

sections.heading: Physics-Aware World Models Unlock Humanoid Potential
sections.summary: By pairing contact wrench prediction with known rigid-body dynamics, DynaMimic resolves the error accumulation issue that plagued prior implicit world models during support transitions. Achieving major gains across benchmarks and demonstrating floor recovery, cartwheels, and vaulting on real hardware, it establishes a new standard for model-based RL.
sections.details:
The core takeaway of this paper is straightforward: there is no need to make neural networks brute-force their way into learning the laws of motion that physics already understands.

DynaMimic delegates only hard-to-predict contact wrenches and small residual forces to the network, leaving state evolution to classical rigid-body dynamics. This division of labor provides tracking accuracy and stability that far surpass conventional differentiable world models like SuperMimic. It cuts flat-ground tracking error by 18.6%, and by conditioning on terrain height maps, reduces errors by around 10% to 15% on environmental contact tasks like parkour and stair climbing.

Moreover, successfully executing complex behaviors such as floor recovery, cartwheels, and box vaults on the real A3 humanoid proves that this hybrid approach is not just a simulation trick, but a powerful paradigm that holds up in the real world.

takeaways: Dividing the workload—computing known rigid-body dynamics analytically while using neural networks only for unknown contact forces—dramatically improves world model accuracy and stability.
Using contact wrenches calculated internally by the simulator as supervision targets (without extra manual annotations) allows the model to accurately learn load distributions across feet and hands.
Directly embedding physical constraints (such as non-negative normal forces and friction cones) into the output layer prevents non-physical or explosive force predictions in the world model.

Policy gradient training inside a differentiable world model offers vastly superior computational efficiency over model-free RL, making it possible to train real-robot deployable acrobatic motions on a single GPU.
limitations: Candidate support links where contact forces can occur must be pre-specified manually (15 links), leaving open challenges for handling extreme motions with unexpected contacts (e.g., forearms or back).
Because simulator contact wrenches serve as supervision, the world model risks inheriting simulation artifacts and solver-specific biases.
Terrain representation relies on a robot-centric 2.5D height map, making it unable to handle fully 3D overhang structures such as enclosed tunnels or low bars to crawl under.
